## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- Tell a born-digital PDF from a scanned one and pick the extraction
  method that fits.
- Extract text and tables from a born-digital PDF.
- Run OCR on a scanned page, and send a page image to a vision model.
- Rebuild a table that runs across several pages.
- Reconcile the rows you extracted with the totals printed on the page.
- Recognize the two ways extraction fails: rows that go missing and
  numbers a model invents.

## What we cover {#coverage}

- [Correia, Luck & Verner (QJE, 2026)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjaf044)
  ran OCR (software that reads the letters in a page image and writes
  them out as text) on national-bank balance sheets in the Comptroller
  of the Currency's annual reports up to 1941, re-read the output by
  hand wherever assets did not equal liabilities plus capital, and added
  later records to build a bank panel from 1863 to 2024 showing that
  failures are predictable.
  [Donaldson (AER, 2018)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20101199) built
  district-level series of crop prices, output, rainfall and trade from
  colonial India's printed government records, never digitized before,
  and showed that railroads cut trade costs and raised real incomes.
  [Hanlon (REStat, 2024)](https://doi.org/10.1162/rest_a_01190)
  digitized a century of weekly London death counts from the Registrar
  General's printed reports, dated heavy fogs from the reports' daily
  weather notes, and estimated the deaths that fog-trapped pollution
  caused. Archives still hold many tables nobody has turned into data.
- Born-digital and scanned PDFs. A born-digital file is made by software
  and stores its words in a text layer you can select, search and copy.
  A scan is a picture of a page and holds no text until OCR runs; at a
  low resolution (dots per inch), OCR misreads more characters.
- Table extraction (pulling a printed table's rows and columns into a
  data frame) from born-digital files, OCR on scans, and a vision model,
  an AI model that takes a picture of a page and returns its text or
  table. Layout detection locates columns, rows, headings and footnotes
  before anything is read.
- Multi-page tables that run across page breaks: headers that repeat,
  rows split across a break, and footnote markers (symbols attached to a
  value) mixed into the numbers.
- In class: handwritten historical records, such as old restaurant
  menus with prices, census pages or ship logbooks, read by a vision
  model and compared with transcriptions volunteers typed by hand.
- Choosing between OCR, a vision model and hand entry, by the number of
  pages and what an error would cost the analysis. Hand entry is usually
  double keyed: two people type the same table, and every cell where
  they differ is re-read against the page.
- The two common failures. Partial extraction drops rows without
  warning, and fabrication returns a plausible number that is not on the
  page. Reconcile the extracted rows with the total row most statistical
  tables print, and verify that a balance sheet obeys its accounting
  identity (a relation that must hold exactly, such as assets equal to
  liabilities plus capital). A sum that falls short points to dropped
  rows, and a cell that breaks the identity points to a misread or
  invented number.
